title: Basil and the Berry Boat
markdown:
There was once a little bear cub named Basil. Basil was a good cub. He loved his mama and his papa. And he especially loved anything sweet and juicy. But Basil had a little wiggle in his tummy whenever he thought about the big blue lake near their cozy den. And in the very middle of that lake was a tiny island bursting with the biggest, reddest, yummiest berries you ever did see. They looked like bright jewels on green velvet.

Basil would often sit by the water’s edge. His nose would twitch. His fluffy brown fur caught the spots of sun that peeked through the tall pine trees. He imagined popping those berries into his mouth — a burst of sweet tangy goodness that would make his whole body tingle. But the water looked so wide and so wet. He’d dip a tiny paw in. A shiver would race up his furry back. His whiskers would quiver.

“It’s much too big, Tip,” he’d sigh to his friend, voice a little shaky.

Tip was a dragonfly: fast and buzzing, emerald-green, wings like tiny colourful windows. Tip wasn’t afraid of much. He loved to dart and dive and dance on the breeze.

“Nonsense, Basil!” He’d do a fast circle, leaving a trail of shiny bits. “It’s just water! And those berries look like they’re waiting for you to gobble them up!”

How does a small bear cub, a little timid about water, get to a berry island in the middle of a big blue lake? It was a puzzle, for sure.

One sunny morning, as Basil sat by a babbling stream that giggled its way toward the lake, he spotted it: snagged on a stray twig, the most enormous leaf-like leaf he had ever seen. Wide and green and strong enough for a bear cub to sit on. A perfect little boat.

“Tip!” His eyes grew as round as saucers. “Look! A leaf-boat!”

Tip zipped over and landed on Basil’s nose for a ticklish moment. “By my wings! That’s absolutely perfect! We can sail to Berry Island on that!”

But the leaf-boat was just across the stream. Not a deep stream for grown-ups. To Basil it looked fast and moving. Tip had a twinkle in his many, many eyes.

“Don’t you worry your furry head. I’ll help you. We’ll nudge it closer with a strong twig. We’ll be a team!”

With lots of pushing and little unhappy noises from Basil, they guided the giant leaf-boat to their side. Basil climbed aboard, very, very carefully, and sat right in the middle, paws gripping the edge. Tip hovered above, ready to be captain, wings a steady hum.

As the leaf-boat got into the moving water, oh dear! It spun! The water rushed around them, gurgling and giggling as if it were playing a trick. Basil held on tight. His fur bristled. His chest felt tight. Oops! A small woven basket of their lunch slipped overboard and tumbled downstream with a splash.

“Oh no!” Basil cried.

“Don’t fret, my friend!” Tip looked a little worried himself as he watched their lunch float away. “We still have enough! And the berries await! They’re even more delicious than those!” He pointed a tiny determined leg toward the big lake, sun shining on the water.

Soon the stream met the wide space of the lake. Their leaf-boat drifted out onto the shining blue. Basil’s tummy did a little somersault. His paws felt clammy. It was so wide! It seemed to go on forever.

“Are you sure, Tip?” he whispered, barely a squeak.

Just then a big puff of wind blew across the water. It caught their leaf-boat and sent it rocking to the side. Basil wobbled. A real shake this time. Worry washed over him, colder than the lake. He squeezed his eyes shut. His little bear nose twitched.

“We’ll never get there, Tip. It’s too far. It’s too big.”

Tip buzzed close to his ear, wings a comforting sound. “Now, now, Basil. Think of those berries. Think of the sweet juicy taste. Imagine them bursting in your mouth. And think of us, together. We’re a team, remember? We can do it. We just need to paddle a little harder. You use your paws, and I’ll buzz with all my might!”

Basil opened his eyes. Tip was right. They were a team. He’d paddle with his strong paws. Tip would be his speedy guide.

They paddled and buzzed with all their might. After what felt like a very long time, with the sun warming their backs, they saw it. Berry Island! Even more wonderful than Basil had imagined: a tiny green gem covered with bushes full of ruby-red berries, plump and ready for picking.

But as they steered closer to the shore, a grumpy old head popped out of the water. Bartholomew the turtle. His shell was old and bumpy like a stone path.

“Halt!” His voice was like stones tumbling down a hill. “You cannot pass without paying a toll. One shiny pebble, or a bite of food!”

Basil’s heart felt very sad. They only had a few sticky honeycombs left, the ones that hadn’t fallen overboard. They had meant them for their big feast on the island. To give them away now felt like losing the whole adventure before it had truly begun. He looked at Tip. A worried frown. Tip’s emerald wings drooped just a tiny bit.

Basil remembered his papa’s gentle words, spoken many times around the cozy fireplace. He looked down at the last, plumpest, honey-sweet berry he had saved, tucked carefully in a little hollow of the leaf-boat. The most beautiful berry. Its sweetness already filled the air.

“Mr. Bartholomew,” Basil said, voice surprisingly steady and clear. “I don’t have a shiny pebble for you. But I have this berry. It’s very sweet. Please, have it. It’s the last one.” He held it out on his paw.

Bartholomew blinked his ancient eyes, slow and thoughtful. He looked at the berry. Then he looked at Basil’s serious kind face. A slow surprising smile spread across his wrinkled snout. “Well, now.” His voice softened like pebbles smoothed by the sea. He gently took the berry with his beak. “That’s mighty kind of you, little bear. Mighty kind indeed. Enjoy your island. The berries are very juicy this year.” With a happy flick of his tail, he swam away into the clear blue water.

Their path was open. They steered right up to the sandy shore. Oh, the smell! Sweet warm berry-scented air filled Basil’s lungs. He tumbled out. Tip followed. And they ate until their tummies were round and full, faces sticky with delicious juice. The berries tasted even better than Basil had dreamed.

As the sun began to set, painting the sky in orange, pink, and purple, they climbed back onto their leaf-boat, happy and full. Basil looked out at the water. A little smile played on his lips. It didn’t seem so big or so scary anymore. It was just water. Beautiful shining water. With Tip buzzing a happy contented tune, the journey home felt much quicker, much smoother, and much, much sweeter. The last berry was gone. The lake still shone. Basil’s paws, still a little sticky, kept paddling anyway.
